Parody

/PAIR-uh-dee/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Parody means a humorous imitation of a work, style, or genre, exaggerating its features for comic effect.

The sketch was a parody of glossy cooking shows: the host whispered reverently over plain toast, drizzled it with bottled tap water, and demanded dramatic close-ups of the butter.

Worked Example

For the talent show, the seniors performed a parody of a nature documentary, supplying hushed, awestruck voice-over for the freshman hallway: 'Here we observe the ninth-grader in its natural habitat, foraging for a working pencil.'

A parody copies a recognizable style — here, the reverent hush of nature documentaries — and pushes its signature features past the point of seriousness. The comedy comes from the whole borrowed style, not from one overstated claim.

How Parody Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

spoof

spoof: a playful comic copy of something familiar

lampoon

lampoon: a mocking version that ridicules its target

send-up

send-up: a lighthearted mockery of a familiar style

Antonyms

tribute

tribute: a work made to honor its subject sincerely

homage

homage: a respectful nod to an admired work

How Strong Is It? — impression → parody → burlesque

impression vs. parody

impression vs. parody: An impression playfully copies one person's voice or mannerisms; a parody rebuilds a whole work or genre for comic effect.

burlesque vs. parody

burlesque vs. parody: A burlesque blows the target up into full theatrical ridicule, mocking it from start to finish.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of parody.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — par-

Prefix — par-: beside, alongside — often with a mocking twist (Greek para-, trimmed before a vowel)

Root — -ody

Root — -ody: song (from Greek oide, the same root that sings inside ode)

Put it together

Put it together: Par- (beside, alongside — Greek para-, trimmed before a vowel) + -ody (song — Greek oide, the same root that sings inside ode): a parody is, at its roots, 'a song sung beside' the original — a piece that runs alongside a familiar work, close enough to recognize and twisted enough to make you laugh.

Use the root in a new word: rhapsody

Use the root in a new word: rhapsody: The violinist closed with a rhapsody, a free-flowing piece that wandered from folk tunes to thunderous chords.

Root Check

Word Choice

Neutral; common in reviews, media criticism, and everyday talk about comedy.

Use parody for a whole comic send-up of a recognizable work, style, or genre — a sketch mocking cooking shows, a song mimicking overwrought ballads. A parody copies its target's signature features and pushes them past the point of seriousness. (Parody often relies on exaggeration — this unit's word Exaggeration — but a single overstated claim by itself is not a parody.)
